Title: Thiols Rule on EGaIn: Competitive Interfacial Chemistry for Electrochemical Biosensing
Authors: Tiantai Wen, Zhiheng Zhang, Yifan Gu, Beixin Chen, Guozhen Liu
Topics: Sensors & Wearables, Electronics & Circuits, Biomedical, Surface & Interface Science
Abstract: Abstract Eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) is a liquid metal of growing interest for interfacial biosensing, yet the competitive affinity of common functional groups toward its native oxide-covered surface remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically probe the relative binding of thiol (−SH), carboxyl (−COOH), and amino (−NH2) groups on EGaIn using two bifunctional aromatic ligands sharing a thiol anchor: p-mercaptobenzoic acid (PMBA) and p-aminothiophenol (PATP). Spectroscopic and microscopic analyses confirm stable ligand retention, while EDC/NHS-based fluorescence labeling reveals that thiol-mediated anchoring clearly predominates. Subsequent gold nanoparticle (AuNP) functionalization and electrochemical interrogation demonstrate that ligand identity critically governs charge-transfer kinetics and AuNP accessibility. Among the interfaces evaluated, EGaIn-PATP-Au exhibits the lowest charge-transfer resistance (1.65 kΩ) and highest interfacial conductance, achieving a 7.58-fold enhancement over bare EGaIn. Deposited onto a glassy carbon electrode, this optimized interface enables specific detection of dopamine with concentration-dependent responses from 0 to 10 μM in PBS and artificial sweat, underscoring its wearable sensing potential. Collectively, these findings establish a robust platform for resolving competitive functional-group interactions at EGaIn interfaces and provide a ligand-engineering strategy for the rational design of liquid-metal electrochemical sensors.
Summary: Collectively, these findings establish a robust platform for resolving competitive functional-group interactions at EGaIn interfaces and provide a ligand-engineering strategy for the rational design of liquid-metal electrochemical sensors.

Title: Ultrastretchable Liquid-Metal Reinforced Polyelectrolyte Hydrogel Sensors for Multichannel Gesture Recognition and Robotic-Hand Control
Authors: Hui Chen, Xuqing Song, Yaming Hu, Xiangning Lu, Tianchi Chen
Topics: Sensors & Wearables, Microfluidics, Electronics & Circuits, Stretchable & Flexible Electronics, Surface & Interface Science
Abstract: Abstract With the development of wearable devices, human-motion monitoring, and human–machine interaction technologies, flexible sensing materials with high stretchability, rapid response, high sensitivity, and cyclic stability are increasingly required. To address conductive-pathway instability under large and repeated deformation, interfacial failure associated with layered liquid-metal/hydrogel architectures, and the difficulty in balancing mechanical deformability with sensing performance, this work reports a liquid-metal-reinforced polyelectrolyte hydrogel based on (2-(acryloyloxy)ethyl)trimethylammonium chloride (AETC) and eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) microdroplets. EGaIn was ultrasonically dispersed in water, introduced into an aqueous AETC precursor, and immobilized within the poly(AETC) network through UV-induced radical polymerization, yielding a bulk-dispersed AETC@LM hydrogel, where AETC@LM denotes an AETC-derived polyelectrolyte hydrogel containing dispersed EGaIn microdroplets. The effects of liquid-metal content on the morphology, chemical structure, mechanical properties, water retention, adhesion, and electromechanical sensing performance of the hydrogels were systematically investigated. Among the investigated formulations, LM200, prepared with 200 μL of the liquid-metal dispersion, exhibited the most favorable overall performance. It sustained a maximum tensile strain of approximately 3000% and provided strain sensing over 0–900%. Piecewise least-squares linear fitting of the strain response yielded gauge factors of 1.4 and 11.3 in the low- and high-strain regions, respectively. Similarly, piecewise least-squares linear fitting of the pressure response yielded sensitivities of 8.07 kPa–1 over approximately 0–7 kPa and 0.68 kPa–1 over approximately 8–25 kPa. LM200 retained approximately 95% of its initial mass after four weeks of ambient storage and exhibited adhesion to different substrates, with the highest adhesion strength observed on wood. The sensor showed response and recovery times of 0.24 and 0.18 s, respectively, and maintained repeatable resistance responses over 600 tensile cycles at 50% strain. Furthermore, five LM200 sensors were integrated into a five-channel smart glove. A ResNet50-based residual-learning model classified ten representative gestures from the acquired multichannel signals, which were also mapped to corresponding robotic-hand postures. The principal innovation of this work is the material-to-system integration of a bulk-dispersed liquid-metal/AETC polyelectrolyte architecture with strain–pressure dual-mode sensing and machine-learning-assisted multichannel gesture recognition. This integrated strategy establishes a structure–property–application relationship for liquid-metal-reinforced polyelectrolyte hydrogels and provides an experimental basis for large-deformation wearable sensing and intelligent human–machine interaction.

Title: MXene conductive hydrogel for uniform electric field wound healing
Authors: Xiaojiang Yang, Shiwen Shen, Yao Li, Weiying Zheng, Negar Javanmardi, et al.
Topics: Sensors & Wearables, Electronics & Circuits, Biomedical, Surface & Interface Science, Fabrication & Processing
Abstract: Flexible conductive materials show considerable potential for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine owing to their favorable mechanical properties, biocompatibility, and electrical characteristics. This study introduces a sequentially bridged, flexible three-layer composite composed of eutectic gallium-indium alloy (EGaIn), MXene, and hydrogel (EMH). This innovative conductive patch exhibits a spatially uniform electric-field distribution and stable electrical performance. The EGaIn layer provides exceptional conductivity, while MXene serves as an active capacitive layer with a high surface area and redox-active sites, facilitating efficient charge storage and redistribution. The synergy between MXene and EGaIn ensures rapid and uniform charge delivery, thereby enhancing electrochemical performance. The hyaluronic acid/polyacrylic acid double-network hydrogel (HPD) imparts remarkable tissue adhesion and mechanical compliance to the EMH patch. Significantly, the EMH demonstrates three times the capacitance compared to the EGaIn-hydrogel (EH), features metallic conductivity (775000 S/m) for swift charge transfer, and maintains stable cycling with less than 2Ω resistance at 235% strain. Its integrated design promise’s reliability under extreme deformation (up to 290% strain), effectively merging MXene’s charge storage capabilities with EGaIn’s strain-tolerant conduction. As an electronic wound dressing, the EMH patch significantly promotes tissue regeneration by facilitating endogenous current conduction that suppresses inflammation and stimulates cell proliferation, thereby enhancing epithelialization and vascularization. This capacitor-integrated layered design offers a promising bioelectronic approach for electric-field-modulated tissue regeneration.
Summary: This study introduces a sequentially bridged, flexible three-layer composite composed of eutectic gallium-indium alloy (EGaIn), MXene, and hydrogel (EMH).
